content: Infantile papular acrodermatitis, also known as Gianotti-Crosti syndrome, is a dermatological reaction to a viral infection. The most commonly implicated viruses are Hepatitis B and Epstein-Barr virus. Other viruses that have been associated with this condition include Hepatitis A, non-A-non-B Hepatitis, cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, adenovirus, enterovirus, rotavirus, rubella, HIV, parainfluenza, parvovirus B19, and respiratory syncytial virus. The condition is named after Ferdinando Gianotti and Agostino Crosti, who first described it. Causes The primary causes of infantile papular acrodermatitis are Hepatitis B and Epstein-Barr virus. Other viruses that may contribute include Hepatitis A, non-A-non-B Hepatitis, cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, adenovirus, enterovirus, rotavirus, rubella, HIV, parainfluenza, parvovirus B19, and respiratory syncytial virus. Differential Diagnosis Infantile papular acrodermatitis must be distinguished from other conditions, including: Acrodermatitis enteropathica Erythema infectiosum Erythema multiforme Hand-foot-and-mouth disease Henoch-Schönlein purpura Kawasaki disease Lichen planus Papular urticaria Papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome Scabies Epidemiology and Demographics This condition primarily affects infants and young children. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Infantile papular acrodermatitis is a self-limiting condition. The rash typically resolves spontaneously within 15 to 60 days. Complications, if they occur, are usually due to associated conditions rather than the rash itself. Diagnosis The diagnosis of infantile papular acrodermatitis is clinical and based on specific criteria: 1. The patient must exhibit all positive clinical features during at least one clinical encounter. 2. The patient must not exhibit any negative clinical features during all clinical encounters related to the rash. 3. No differential diagnosis should be deemed more likely than infantile papular acrodermatitis based on clinical judgment. 4. If a skin biopsy is performed, histopathological findings must be consistent with the condition. Positive clinical features include: Monomorphic, flat-topped, pink-brown papules or papulovesicles measuring 1–10 mm in diameter. Involvement of at least three of the following four sites: cheeks, buttocks, extensor surfaces of the forearms, and extensor surfaces of the legs. Symmetrical distribution. Duration of at least 10 days. Negative clinical features include: Extensive truncal lesions. Scaly lesions. Symptoms The condition is characterized by a papular or papulovesicular rash, primarily affecting the face and distal aspects of the four limbs. Less prominent truncal lesions do not exclude the diagnosis. Other symptoms may include itching and asthenia (generalized weakness). Physical Examination The rash is papular or papulovesicular and is predominantly located on the face and distal extremities. Laboratory Findings Elevated liver transaminases may be detected, but bilirubin levels (both conjugated and unconjugated) typically remain normal. The absence of elevated transaminases does not rule out the diagnosis. Hepatitis virus serology or Hepatitis B surface antigen testing may be performed. Screening for Epstein-Barr virus antibodies may be indicated. Serum zinc levels may be tested if acrodermatitis enteropathica is suspected. Skin biopsy may be performed for confirmation. Treatment Infantile papular acrodermatitis is a benign and self-limiting condition, so treatment is often unnecessary. Management focuses on controlling itching, providing symptomatic relief, and preventing complications. For itching, oral antihistamines or soothing lotions such as calamine or zinc oxide may be used. If associated conditions, such as streptococcal infections, are present, antibiotics may be required.
